deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 155 continues a German prose narrative of Hellenistic history, apparently notes from a history lecture or a reading. The thread runs on from fol. 154 (Demetrius' naval victory at Cyprian Salamis) into fol. 156 (Cassander, and the coalition against Antigonus in 302). In modern summary the page says:

- Antigonus took the royal title and founded Antigonia in Syria; Ptolemy also took the royal title.
- Antigonus hoped to conquer Egypt and made great preparations. He planned to invade by land with 80,000 men while Demetrius attacked from the sea.
- The fleet was almost entirely wrecked by a storm, and the army largely melted away through desertions. Antigonus had to abandon the expedition. This was the Egyptian campaign of 306 BC.
- Since he could not take Egypt, Rhodes was made to pay for it. Demetrius received command of the fleet with 40,000 men.
- He made himself master of the island and strained every resource to take the city as well. Part of the wall had already fallen, and Demetrius pushed as far as the forum (marketplace). He was driven out again and had to withdraw from the city. This was the siege of Rhodes, 305–304 BC; the narrative continues on fol. 156.

There is nothing to reconstruct mathematically. The figures (80,000 land troops; 40,000 men against Rhodes) agree with the standard ancient account (Diodorus Siculus XX).
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematical content.

Historically, the narrative matches the standard account (Diodorus XX.73–76 and XX.81–99). The 80,000 infantry for the Egyptian invasion and roughly 40,000 men for the siege of Rhodes are the traditional figures.
Minor simplification: the notes compress the siege of Rhodes, which lasted about a year, into a single breach-and-repulse episode.
